Female Rusty jobfish attain a maximum recorded total length of 110 cm [Li = 110 cm], a size that places them among the larger lutjanids in the Indo-Pacific region. This ultimate length is achieved only after many years of growth, and the corresponding asymptotic wet weight has been estimated at 14,800 g [Wwi = 14,800 g] based on length-weight relationships derived from sampled populations. In contrast, the onset of reproductive capability occurs at a considerably smaller body size. Puberty in females is reached at a total length of 60 cm [Lp = 60 cm], at which point the average individual weighs approximately 2,500 g [Wwp = approximately 2,500 g]. This marked difference between the size at first maturity and the ultimate size suggests a prolonged adult growth phase following reproductive onset, a pattern consistent with the iteroparous strategy observed in many deep-water snappers.

The pelagic eggs of Aphareus rutilans are quite small, with an average egg diameter of 0.82 mm. From this measurement, the calculated wet weight at birth, representing the mass of the newly fertilized ovum, is approximately 0.00029 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00029 grams]. This negligible initial mass highlights the extremely altricial state of the offspring at the moment of spawning. Development proceeds rapidly within the warm waters these fish inhabit. At a stable temperature of 18.4 °C [T = 18.4 °C], the age at birth, defined as the period from fertilization to the hatching of the yolk-sac larva, is about 5 days [ab = about 5 days]. This brief embryonic phase is typical of tropical marine teleosts that produce numerous small, pelagic eggs.

Data for the gonado-somatic index in this species are often inferred from closely related taxa. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) is estimated at approximately 2.7% [GSI = approximately 2.7%], measured at an ambient temperature of 18.4 °C [T = 18.4 °C]. This reproductive strategy stands in contrast to that of some congeners that exhibit a more concentrated, single pulse of gamete production.

Longevity is a key axis of the life history for this species. Under the prevailing thermal conditions of its habitat at 18.4 °C [T = 18.4 °C], the maximum lifespan for Aphareus rutilans is considerable. Field records and otolith-based aging studies suggest that individuals can live for up to approximately 30 years [am = up to approximately 30 years] at a temperature of 18.4 °C [T = 18.4 °C]. This extended lifespan aligns with the species' relatively slow growth rate and late maturity. Such a life-history profile, characterized by high longevity and a delayed onset of reproduction, makes the Rusty jobfish particularly vulnerable to overfishing, as the removal of large, old individuals can rapidly deplete the reproductive potential of the population.

The juvenile phase of the Rusty jobfish is characterized by rapid somatic growth as the fish recruits to deeper reef habitats following its pelagic larval stage. Young individuals face intense predation pressure, and the transition to benthic habitats is a key bottleneck. The diet of this species consists primarily of small fish and cephalopods, reflecting its position as a mid-level predator in the mesophotic reef ecosystem. Fishery landings data indicate that the species is primarily caught by hook-and-line gear, and its slow growth and late maturity make it particularly susceptible to overexploitation. Ongoing research into the reproductive biology and population dynamics of this lutjanid is crucial for developing sustainable harvest strategies.
